title: {{NAME}} and the Menagerie of Forgotten Machines
moral: A world works best when its most powerful things are guided by those who listen to the smallest ones.

pages.content: The Royal Menagerie of Forgotten Machines occupied the eastern wing of the palace and the whole of the garden behind it, and it had been sealed for fifty years by order of the previous monarch, who had found machines disconcerting. The current ruler, Princess Asha, had unsealed it three days ago on the grounds that disconcerting things were often the most interesting, and had not been seen since. {{NAME}} arrived at the menagerie's iron gates to find them open and a small, insistent monkey sitting on the gatepost. The monkey was holding a note. The note, in very elegant handwriting, said: the large one near the fountain has got stuck again, please bring the adjustable wrench from the third shelf. {{NAME}} looked at the monkey. The monkey looked back with the expression of someone who has delivered many notes and has opinions about the quality of the responses. {{NAME}} stepped through the gate into a garden full of extraordinary, sleeping shapes: machines in every animal form, still and rust-touched, draped in climbing roses and patient moss. Somewhere near the fountain, something was whirring.

pages.content: Princess Asha was exactly where the note had implied: at the fountain, which was ringed by the largest machine in the menagerie, a mechanical elephant whose brass hide was etched with intricate leaf-patterns and whose eyes were twin lanterns of amber glass. The elephant was attempting to take a step and could not. Its right foreleg gear assembly had locked, and the mechanism was cycling helplessly, a soft, urgent clicking. Asha had her head inside the leg panel and her voice was a muffled stream of specific, knowledgeable instructions she was giving to herself because she was out of hands. She was small and precise and completely absorbed, her dark hair held back by what appeared to be a circuit wire. She registered {{NAME}}'s arrival by extending one hand backward without looking up. He slapped the adjustable wrench into it without a word. The wrench vanished into the panel. Three deliberate sounds. Then silence. The elephant took one step, enormous and measured, and the amber eyes lit. Asha emerged from the panel with oil on her nose and an expression of pure satisfaction. She noticed the oil. She left it where it was.

pages.content: Asha had been slowly waking the menagerie machines for three days, and the problem she had not anticipated was this: when you wake a hundred mechanical animals that have been asleep for fifty years, they are all very confused at once. The mechanical wolves were chasing the mechanical deer in perfect good faith, the same way they had been programmed to, but the real animals, who had moved into the menagerie garden in the fifty years of its sealing, were finding this alarming. A family of actual rabbits was perched on top of the dormant mechanical rhino and refusing to come down. Real sparrows were dive-bombing the mechanical hawk, which was performing its hunting display in loops and could not be reasoned with. The monkey from the gate was attempting to mediate everything simultaneously and visibly losing the will to do so. {{NAME}} and Asha divided the problem between them with the efficiency of two people who think in compatible shapes. Asha went to the mechanical systems; {{NAME}} went to the animals. In forty minutes, the rabbits were relocated to a safe burrow beneath the old wall, the sparrows were bribed with seeds, and the hawk had been sent through a diagnostic cycle that slowed its display by half.

pages.content: The hardest machine to wake was the one Asha cared about most: a mechanical hummingbird, palm-sized, made from silver and copper and glass, suspended from the old lime tree on a filament so fine it was invisible. She had found the restoration manual for it that morning, and it required something none of the other machines had needed: not a tool, but a sound. A specific frequency, produced by the right voice at the right pitch, that would unlock the primary spring. Asha had been trying for three days. Her pitch was good, but not quite exact. The monkey had tried. The result had been memorable. {{NAME}} did not know if he had the right voice. He stood under the lime tree with the manual in his hands and read the notation for the frequency, and then simply opened his mouth and tried, the way you try a locked door with a found key: not expecting it to work, but trying with complete sincerity anyway. The hummingbird sprang to life. Its wings were a blur so fast they were invisible, only their sound remaining, a hum like a plucked string. Asha made a sound that was very small and not at all royal. Then she squared her shoulders and pretended it had not happened.

pages.content: By evening the menagerie had found its balance, the mechanical animals moving in their programs while the real animals navigated around them with the pragmatic confidence of creatures who have decided that extraordinary things are simply part of where they live. The mechanical elephant had adopted a position near the garden gate and was performing what appeared to be a slow, stately patrol. The rabbits had come back out and were running figure-eights between its legs with an energy that suggested they had decided it was excellent sport. The mechanical hummingbird was doing something that had not been in the manual: hovering near the flowers and performing what could only be described as a dance. Asha was watching it with the expression of someone who has built something and then discovered it has become more than what they made. {{NAME}} sat on the fountain's edge, boots off, feet in the water, watching the last light change the brass animals from gold to copper to deep amber. He was asleep before Asha finished her notes, his burgundy jacket folded under his head, the monkey sitting on his feet like a paperweight. In the lime tree above him, the hummingbird still danced, its wings a sound like a secret.
